content: Perilla is a genus of annual herbs belonging to the mint family, Lamiaceae. In regions with mild climates, the plant is capable of self-reseeding. The most commonly cultivated species is Perilla frutescens var. japonica, also known as shiso, which is predominantly grown in India and East Asia. Botanists generally classify the green-leafed and purple-leafed varieties as separate species. The leaves of perilla resemble those of stinging nettle but are slightly rounder in shape. This plant is also widely referred to as the beefsteak plant. In North America, it is increasingly recognized by its Japanese name, shiso, in addition to the general term perilla. The essential oils of perilla contribute to its strong flavor, which is often compared to the intensity of mint or fennel. The plant is considered rich in minerals and vitamins, exhibits anti-inflammatory properties, and is believed to aid in preserving and sterilizing other foods. In Nepal and parts of India, it is known as silam, and its seeds are ground with chili and tomatoes to create a savory dip or side dish. Perilla is sometimes referred to as purple mint, Japanese basil, or wild coleus, though it is not closely related to mint, basil, or coleus. In traditional Chinese medicine, perilla (known as 紫苏 in Chinese) has been used for its medicinal properties. It has been shown to stimulate interferon activity, thereby enhancing the immune system. In Japan, perilla is called shiso (紫蘇). The green variety is referred to as aoba (green leaf), ōba (big leaf), or aosiso, and it is commonly eaten with sashimi (sliced raw fish) or used in salads, spaghetti, and meat or fish dishes. It is also used as a flavorful herb in various recipes, including as a pizza topping, where it was initially used as a substitute for basil. The purple variety, known as akashiso, is used to make umeboshi (pickled ume) or combined with ume paste in sushi to create umeshiso maki. The inflorescence of shiso is called hojiso, and its young leaves and flower buds are used for pickling in Japan and Taiwan. In Vietnamese cuisine, a variety of perilla similar to the Japanese hojiso is used, but it has greenish-bronze coloring on the top side and purple on the underside. The leaves are smaller and have a much stronger fragrance than hojiso. In Vietnamese, it is called tía tô, derived from the characters 紫蘇 (pronounced tử tô in standard Vietnamese). It is typically eaten as a garnish in rice vermicelli dishes (bún) and various stews and simmered dishes. In Indonesia, perilla is known as kemangi. The variety used is similar to the one found in Thailand. The seeds collected from the flowers are called selasih and are often added to drinks. In Korea, the plant is called deulkkae or tŭlkkae (들깨), and the same term is used to refer to its seeds, which have numerous applications in Korean cuisine, as do the leaves (kkaennip, 깻잎). Despite the literal translations of deulkkae (wild sesame) and kkaennip (sesame leaf), perilla is not closely related to sesame. English translations of Korean cookbooks sometimes use these terms. Cans of pickled kkaennip are widely available in Korean stores worldwide, often with ground red pepper placed between the leaves. The leaves' essential oils give them a strong taste, and fresh leaves have an aroma reminiscent of apples and mint. They are commonly eaten in salads. The flavor of Korean perilla is distinct from Japanese perilla, and the leaves are larger, rounder, flatter, and less serrated, often with violet coloring on the underside. Perilla oil (deulgireum, 들기름) is extracted from the seeds and has a rich taste and scent, somewhat resembling dark sesame oil (chamgireum, 참기름). The oil cake left after extraction can be used as animal feed. Perilla seeds can be cooked with meals, roasted, crushed to intensify their flavor, or mixed with sesame and salt. The essential oil extracted from perilla leaves through steam distillation contains various chemical compounds, which may vary depending on the species. The most abundant compound, comprising about 50–60% of the oil, is perillaldehyde, which is primarily responsible for the aroma and taste of perilla. Other common terpenes include limonene, caryophyllene, and farnesene. Among the known chemotypes of perilla, PA (main component: perillaldehyde) is the only one used for culinary purposes. Other chemotypes include PK (perilla ketone), EK (elsholtzia ketone), PL (perillene), PP (phenylpropanoids such as myristicin, dillapiole, and elemicin), C (citral), and a type rich in rosefuran. Perilla ketone is toxic to some animals. When cattle and horses consume purple mint (of the PK chemotype) while grazing, the perilla ketone can cause pulmonary edema, leading to a condition sometimes referred to as perilla mint toxicosis. Perilla oil is obtained by pressing the seeds, which contain 35–45% oil. In parts of Asia, perilla oil is used as an edible oil valued more for its medicinal benefits than its flavor. It is a very rich source of the omega-3 fatty acid alpha-linolenic acid. As a drying oil similar to tung oil or linseed oil, perilla oil has been used in paints, varnishes, linoleum, printing ink, lacquers, and protective waterproof coatings on cloth. It can also be used as a fuel. The oxime of perillaldehyde (perillartine) is used as an artificial sweetener in Japan, as it is approximately 2,000 times sweeter than sucrose.
